entry.title: AI Agent Monitoring Checklist: What to Watch in Production
entry.summary: Monitoring an AI agent in production means watching what it did, what it cost, whether the output was any good and whether anything suspicious happened. This checklist sets out 16 items across six areas, maps each to OpenTelemetry signals where they exist, and cites the NCSC and OWASP guidance on logging and agent risks.

entry.title: AI Agent Statistics 2026: Adoption, Spend, Reliability and Failure Rates
entry.summary: Agents are now common in large companies but rarely run alone. Surveys put agents in production at most large US firms, while McKinsey finds about two in ten respondents scaling agents enterprise-wide. Independent measurements show long tasks completed at 50% success and much shorter ones at 80%, and Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027. Every figure here carries its source, sample and date.

entry.title: AI Agents for Small Business: What Works Now and What to Skip
entry.summary: Small businesses are adopting AI quickly, and about a quarter of small-business AI users already use agentic tools. The tasks that work are frequent, internal and easy to check: meeting preparation, call summaries, record clean-up and first drafts. Anything that sends to customers, sets prices or changes access should stay with a person. Surveyed small businesses that pay for AI report a median of $250 a month.

entry.title: AI Assistant Pricing Compared (2026): Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for Business
entry.summary: Business AI assistant seats list at $20 to $21 per user per month on annual billing at Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, with premium seats at $100, while Google includes Gemini in Workspace plans from $7. The seat price is only part of the cost: monthly billing, usage limits, credits and metered agents sit beside it.

entry.title: AI Audit Trail Checklist: What to Log for Every AI Decision
entry.summary: An AI audit trail lets a firm rebuild any AI-assisted decision: what the system was asked, what it saw, what it did, who checked it and what happened. This checklist sets out the system-level and decision-level fields to log, the regulatory text behind each, the retention rules that apply and a test that shows whether the trail works.

entry.title: AI Credits Explained: How Credit-Based Pricing Works and How to Budget
entry.summary: AI credits are a prepaid or metered currency that a vendor converts into AI work at its own burn rates. They let one price cover many features, and they move forecasting risk to the buyer. Budget by converting credits into cost per task, and negotiate rollover, true-up and alerts before you commit.

entry.title: AI Governance Framework Template for Mid-Size Financial Firms
entry.summary: An AI governance framework sets who owns AI risk, what AI the firm runs, how each use is tiered and approved, how people oversee it, how vendors are controlled and what records prove it worked. This template sets out eleven components for a mid-size financial firm, each anchored to NIST's AI RMF, the OCC's November 2026 framework, the FCA's October 2026 review, SR 26-2, DORA and the EU AI Act.

entry.title: AI Gross Margin Explained: Why AI Products Earn Less Than SaaS
entry.summary: AI gross margin is revenue less the direct cost of serving AI features, chiefly inference, compute and human review, divided by revenue. Investor surveys put AI product margins between about 25% and 60%, against 80% to 85% for SaaS licence revenue. The gap comes from a real cost per use, and it is widest on heavy users of flat-priced seats.

entry.title: AI Pricing Statistics 2026: Models, Price Points and Trends
entry.summary: A sourced reference of AI pricing statistics for 2026. Hybrid pricing reached 37% of software companies, consumption pricing 42% and outcome pricing 23% of AI vendors, and AI credits 29%. AI product margins averaged 45% in 2025. Every figure is dated and sourced, and most come from investor or vendor surveys, which we label.

entry.title: Business Decision Records vs Architecture Decision Records
entry.summary: An architecture decision record captures one software design choice with its context, decision, status and consequences. A business decision record applies the same discipline to commercial and operating decisions and adds what engineering records usually skip: one named owner, an expected outcome, a falsifier and a check date, so the decision can be graded and its outcome written back.

entry.title: Decision Record Template: Fields, Example and How to Use It
entry.summary: A decision record template is a fixed set of fields for one decision: what was decided, why, who owns it, its status, the expected outcome, the check date and the falsifier. This guide gives the full template as a table, a filled composite example and the usage rules borrowed from architecture decision records: never edit an accepted record, supersede it.

entry.title: DORA and AI: What the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act Means for AI Systems
entry.summary: DORA regulates ICT rather than AI as such, but AI systems that EU financial entities run or buy are ICT assets and ICT services, so its rules on ICT risk management, logging, incidents, testing and third parties apply to them. The ESAs' July 2026 statement on frontier AI added no obligations but showed how supervisors read the Act. This explainer maps each DORA duty to an AI system.

entry.title: Enterprise AI Adoption Statistics 2026
entry.summary: Most large organisations now use AI somewhere, and fewer than half say it is scaling across the enterprise. Government data shows far lower use across all US businesses, rising sharply with firm size and concentrated in information and finance. Returns lag adoption: McKinsey finds 37% attributing any EBIT impact to AI. Every figure here carries its source, sample and date.

entry.title: Enterprise Brain vs Knowledge Base: What Is the Difference?
entry.summary: A knowledge base stores and retrieves documented answers. An enterprise brain is the whole loop: store, wiring, a record of decisions with reasons and owners, reasoning by models and agents, and outcomes written back. A knowledge base is part of the store and wiring. The difference shows when an AI agent must tell a current decision from a superseded one.

entry.title: EU AI Act Logging Requirements: Articles 12, 19 and 26 Explained
entry.summary: Article 12 of the EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to record events automatically over their lifetime; Articles 19 and 26 require providers and deployers to keep those logs for at least six months, and financial institutions to hold them within their financial services documentation. The Digital Omnibus moved the start date for Annex III systems to 2 December 2027 but left the logging text unchanged.

entry.title: FINRA and AI in 2026: What Broker-Dealers Must Record and Supervise
entry.summary: FINRA has no AI-specific rule. Its technology-neutral rules on supervision, communications and books and records apply to AI tools, and its 2026 oversight report added a section on AI agents with seven named risks. This explainer maps the rules to the records a broker-dealer should keep, the retention periods, and the rule changes in progress.

entry.title: How Much Does an AI Agent Cost? Build, Buy and Run Costs in 2026
entry.summary: Published agent prices run from $0.10 per action to $125 per user per month, and from $0.99 per outcome for support agents. A self-built agent's token bill is usually small; human review, retries and engineering time are not. The number to budget on is cost per successful task, including the people who check the work.

entry.title: How to Build a Company Knowledge Base for AI
entry.summary: A company knowledge base for AI is a curated, permissioned set of authoritative sources that assistants and agents retrieve from. Build it around one set of recurring questions: gather one current copy of each source, structure and tag it, fix permissions before rollout, link the decision records that explain why policies are what they are, and test it against real questions before widening scope.

entry.title: How to Choose an AI Agent Platform: A Buyer's Checklist
entry.summary: An AI agent platform is the software that lets a company build, run and govern agents. Most mid-size firms already own one inside their CRM or productivity suite, so the decision is usually which to switch on, not which to buy. This checklist sets out twelve questions to put to any vendor, the evidence to request, and how to test a platform on your own tasks before signing.

entry.title: How to Document an AI Model for Regulators: A Practical Template
entry.summary: Supervisors want AI documentation that someone outside the build team can read, check and audit. This template sets out twelve sections, from purpose and risk tier to monitoring, change history and decision records, and maps each to SR 26-2, the OCC's November 2026 examiner framework, EU AI Act Annex IV and PRA SS1/23. It also covers vendor models, proportionality and retention.

entry.title: How to Evaluate an AI Agent: Tests, Metrics and Graders
entry.summary: Evaluating an AI agent means testing a multi-step system that acts, not a single answer. The method is a fixed set of real tasks, several trials per task, graders matched to what is being checked, and metrics that capture consistency as well as success. This guide sets out the tests, metrics and graders, with dated guidance from Anthropic, OpenAI, LangChain and Langfuse.

entry.title: How to Negotiate an AI Software Contract: Caps, Credits and Outcome Terms
entry.summary: AI contracts move cost risk into terms that classic software contracts never needed: the billable unit, burn rates, caps, rollover and change notice. Published vendor terms show where the defaults sit. This guide sets out ten clauses with an opening ask, a fallback and a dated precedent for each, and the data to bring to the table.

entry.title: How to Price an AI Product: A Step-by-Step Method
entry.summary: Pricing an AI product starts with cost per completed task, because AI has a real marginal cost that SaaS mostly did not. Choose a value metric that tracks how customers get value, set the price between the cost floor and the buyer's next best alternative, check the margin, and run every change as an experiment with a stop rule.

entry.title: Langfuse vs LangSmith: Which LLM Observability Tool to Choose
entry.summary: Langfuse and LangSmith cover the same core jobs: tracing, evaluation, human review and OpenTelemetry ingestion. They differ in licence, how self-hosting is sold, how usage is billed and how long data is kept at list price. This comparison sets out the facts from both vendors' pages as of 16 November 2026 and the situations where each fits.

entry.title: LLM-as-a-Judge Explained: When Model Graders Work and When They Fail
entry.summary: LLM-as-a-judge is the use of a language model to grade AI outputs against a rubric. Research shows strong judges can agree with people about as often as people agree with each other, and also documents position, verbosity, self-preference and leniency biases. This guide sets out when model graders work, when they fail, what they cost and how to check them.

entry.title: LLM Observability Pricing Compared (2026)
entry.summary: LLM observability platforms bill in different units: tracing units, seats and traces, spans and gigabytes, scores, or model-call spans. This comparison sets out list prices, included usage, overage and retention for five platforms as listed on 16 November 2026, prices a small-team workload, and lists the costs that do not appear on pricing pages.

entry.title: OpenTelemetry GenAI Semantic Conventions Explained
entry.summary: The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions are the open naming standard for traces of model calls, agent runs, tool calls, token use and evaluation scores. They moved to their own repository in June 2026 and every gen_ai attribute is still at Development status. This guide sets out what they define, how vendors use them and what to do while they change.

entry.title: Per-Resolution vs Per-Outcome Pricing: What Changed and What to Check
entry.summary: Per-resolution pricing charges when an AI agent solves the customer's problem. Per-outcome pricing charges for a wider list of results, including handoffs and lead qualification. In 2026 Intercom moved Fin to outcomes and Zendesk moved to verified resolutions, in opposite directions. Buyers should recount last month's conversations under the new rules before renewal.

entry.title: SR 26-2 vs SR 11-7: What Changed in US Model Risk Guidance
entry.summary: SR 26-2 replaced SR 11-7 on 17 April 2026. It raises the relevance threshold to $30 billion in assets, narrows the model definition, drops the annual validation expectation, rewrites effective challenge, gives vendor models their own section and excludes generative and agentic AI. This comparison sets the two side by side and shows which policy clauses to revisit.

entry.title: What Is a Context Graph?
entry.summary: A context graph is a connected record of decision traces, such as the rules applied, exceptions granted, approvals given and precedents used, linked to the people, accounts and documents they concern. The term was popularised by Foundation Capital in December 2025 and vendors now define it in different ways. In lowob's model it captures part of the decision record automatically, but not the expected outcome, falsifier or check date.

entry.title: What Is Organizational Memory, and How AI Changes It
entry.summary: Organizational memory, as Walsh and Ungson defined it in 1991, is stored information from an organization's history that can be brought to bear on present decisions. It lives in people, culture, procedures, structures, workplaces and outside archives, and research led by Linda Argote shows it can decay and resists transfer. AI makes retrieval cheap but adds new risks: answers built on superseded records and summaries that outlive their sources.

entry.title: What Is SR 26-2? The 2026 US Model Risk Guidance Explained
entry.summary: SR 26-2 is the Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management issued by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC on 17 April 2026. It supersedes SR 11-7 and SR 21-8, is most relevant to banks above $30 billion in assets, sets no enforceable standards and places generative and agentic AI outside its scope. This explainer sets out what it covers, what it leaves out and what has happened since.

entry.title: Why AI Agent Projects Fail: The Evidence and How to Avoid It
entry.summary: Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, and S&P Global found 42% of companies abandoning most AI initiatives before production. The causes are consistent across sources: tasks longer than agents can complete reliably, no workflow redesign, value nobody measures, rising running costs, poor data and weak controls. Each has a check a buyer can run before launch.

entry.title: What Is an AI Center of Excellence?
entry.summary: An AI centre of excellence is an internal team that sets standards for AI use, prioritises requests, runs pilots and spreads skills, so adoption is neither fragmented nor ungoverned. Guidance suggests starting centralised and moving to an advisory role as adoption matures. For a mid-size firm it can be two or three people with a clear mandate.

entry.title: What Is Customer Churn?
entry.summary: Customer churn measures how many customers, or how much of their recurring revenue, a firm loses over a period. Logo churn counts customers; gross revenue churn counts lost and downgraded revenue and is the complement of gross revenue retention. Reporting both shows whether losses are concentrated in small or large accounts, and recording the reason for each loss is what lets the next renewal go better.

entry.title: What Is a Buying Committee?
entry.summary: A buying committee, also called a buying group or buying centre, is everyone at a customer who takes part in a purchase decision. Academic work since the 1960s and recent analyst surveys agree it is larger and more conflicted than sellers assume: Forrester found 13 people on average in 2024. For a commercial team the practical step is to record the committee on each opportunity, by role, and to sell to its consensus.

entry.title: What Is a Small Language Model?
entry.summary: A small language model uses the same design as a large one with far fewer parameters, typically under about 10 billion, so it runs on modest hardware at lower cost. It suits narrow, repeated tasks such as classification, extraction and routing. The practical pattern is a mix: small models for routine steps, a large model where open-ended judgment is needed.

entry.title: What Is AI Literacy, and What Does the EU AI Act Require?
entry.summary: AI literacy is the skills and understanding people need to use AI systems in an informed way and to recognise their risks. Article 4 of the EU AI Act makes it a duty for providers and deployers. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 kept the duty but changed it from ensuring a sufficient level to taking measures that support it, with no set level guaranteed for any individual.

entry.title: What Is a Data Processing Agreement for AI Tools?
entry.summary: A data processing agreement is the contract GDPR Article 28 requires when a vendor processes personal data on a company's behalf. For AI tools it decides whether prompts can be used beyond your instructions, which model providers act as sub-processors, and what is deleted at the end. Most vendors publish a standard one.

entry.title: Semantic Layer vs Knowledge Graph
entry.summary: A semantic layer defines metrics and business terms once so every tool calculates them the same way. A knowledge graph stores entities and named relationships so a system can follow connections. Both give AI explicit business meaning; they answer different questions, and most commercial teams need the definitions before the graph.

entry.title: What Is a Quarterly Business Review (QBR)?
entry.summary: A quarterly business review is a scheduled meeting in which a supplier and a customer review results against the goals they agreed, discuss changes in the customer's business and set goals for the next quarter. Done well, it is the main place where renewal evidence is built. Done badly, it is a usage slide deck. Gartner's research on buyer regret shows why the difference matters.

entry.title: What Is Product-Led Growth?
entry.summary: Product-led growth is a go-to-market motion in which people find, try and start paying for a product largely on their own, with sales joining later to expand accounts. Investor benchmarks show it can grow fast but converts only a small share of free users. It fits products that deliver value without a conversation, and breaks when setup, integration or a buying committee stands in the way.

entry.title: Building the Commercial System at 20, 50 and 200 People
entry.summary: Thirty parts describe a full commercial system. No firm should build all of it at once. This capstone maps each part to three sizes, using lowob's scale ladder: at 20 people the job is to write the founder's system down, at 50 to make words mean the same thing across teams, and at 200 to let reasoning travel without its author. For each size it sets out what to own, what to rent and what to leave until the next rung.

entry.title: How to Raise for an Emerging Tech Company: The Complete Guide
entry.summary: Venture totals hit records in 2026, but the money is concentrated: rounds of $100 million or more took 87.5% of US venture dollars in the first half, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell by 42%. This guide brings together lowob's nine fundraising pieces: what each stage is buying, why evidence beats narrative, how to run the round like a sales process, how to diagnose a stall, and what changes for AI, regulated, long-cycle and media companies.

entry.title: Lead Scoring vs Account Scoring
entry.summary: Lead scoring ranks individual people by fit and engagement so sales can work the best leads first. Account scoring ranks companies, combining firmographic fit with the activity of everyone engaged from that company. B2B purchases involve groups, so most firms need both, with the account score deciding priority and the lead score deciding who to contact.

entry.title: SOC 2 vs ISO 27001 for AI Vendors
entry.summary: SOC 2 is an attestation report in which a CPA firm tests a service organisation's controls against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. ISO/IEC 27001 is an international standard for an information security management system, certified by an accredited body. Neither currently tests model behaviour, so buyers of AI tools need both kinds of evidence plus questions of their own.

entry.title: What Is an Open-Weight Model?
entry.summary: An open-weight model publishes its trained parameters so anyone permitted by the licence can run and modify it. That is not the same as open source AI, which the Open Source Initiative's 2024 definition says also requires training code and data information. For a business, open weights trade per-token fees and provider control for hosting, safety and licence work.

entry.title: LTV:CAC vs CAC Payback: Which Unit Economics Metric to Trust
entry.summary: LTV:CAC divides an estimate of a customer's lifetime gross profit by the cost of acquiring them. CAC payback counts the months of gross profit needed to recover that cost. LTV:CAC depends heavily on a churn assumption that young firms cannot yet observe, so payback is usually the safer metric for budget decisions, with LTV:CAC used once retention history exists.

entry.title: What Is an Approval Gate for AI Agents?
entry.summary: An approval gate is the point where an AI agent stops and waits for a person before an action takes effect. OWASP recommends it for high-impact actions, and the main agent frameworks now build it in. The design questions are which actions to gate, who approves, what the approver sees and how the decision is logged.

entry.title: RevOps vs Sales Ops: What Changed and Why It Matters
entry.summary: Sales operations gives the sales team its processes, tools, analytics and plans. Revenue operations extends that work across marketing, sales and customer success, with one set of definitions, data and systems. The change matters more now because AI assistants and agents read across all three functions and inherit every inconsistency between them.

entry.title: Pricing Experiments in B2B
entry.summary: Price is the strongest profit lever most firms have and the one they test least. A 1992 Harvard Business Review analysis of 2,463 companies found a 1% price improvement lifted operating profit by 11.1%, more than any other lever. B2B firms rarely have the volume or the anonymity for consumer-style A/B tests, so this piece sets out the experiments that do work: cohort changes, packaging tests, discount guardrails and stated-preference research, with the record each one needs and the competition-law line not to cross.

entry.title: MCP vs API Integrations: What Changes and What Does Not
entry.summary: A traditional API integration is a fixed path a developer codes against one system. The Model Context Protocol lets an AI application discover a system's tools at run time and lets the model decide when to call them. The API usually still sits underneath, so permissions, data quality and approvals matter as much as before.

entry.title: What Is Synthetic Data?
entry.summary: Synthetic data is artificial data generated by algorithms to reproduce the statistical patterns of real data. It is useful for testing, for training where data is scarce, and for sharing without exposing records. The ICO warns it can still be personal data, and research in Nature shows models trained recursively on generated data degrade.

entry.title: What Is Conversation Intelligence?
entry.summary: Conversation intelligence tools record and transcribe sales calls and meetings, then flag topics such as competitor and pricing mentions, next steps and coaching moments. Salesforce and Gong document typical features and consent settings. Recording law and the EU ban on workplace emotion recognition set limits. The value comes when confirmed commitments move into the CRM and the decision record.

entry.title: What Is an AI SDR?
entry.summary: An AI SDR is software that performs sales development tasks with some autonomy: researching accounts, drafting and sending prospecting emails, answering replies and booking meetings. Salesforce and HubSpot both ship versions. The evaluation questions are less about writing quality than about sending controls, deliverability, consent law and whether the vendor's own claims can be checked.

entry.title: Account Planning for the Top Twenty
entry.summary: Key account programmes underperform with unusual consistency: Gartner found 58% of B2B sales organisations missing quota on key accounts and most rebuilding their programmes repeatedly. The causes are selection by size of spend, plans that are written once, and coordination that stops at the sales team. This piece sets out a selection rule, a one-page plan, a monthly review and the record that makes each plan a set of decisions rather than a document.

entry.title: The Build Order for Healthcare and Life Sciences
entry.summary: Healthcare and life sciences is one of two sectors where The Build Order bends. HIPAA's marketing rules, state consumer health data laws, FDA promotional enforcement and Open Payments reporting mean the walls, the review gate and the record must exist before any commercial agent. The first agent works for the review committee, not the field team, and patient data never reaches the commercial build.

entry.title: What Is a Sales Compensation Plan?
entry.summary: A sales compensation plan is the written set of rules that turns a seller's results into pay. Its main parts are target pay, the split between base and incentive, the upside for over-performance, the measures, the quota and the payout curve. Survey data from WorldatWork and the Alexander Group shows typical choices, and field research shows that design changes behaviour in predictable ways.

entry.title: What Is Entity Resolution?
entry.summary: Entity resolution is the work of deciding which records describe the same real-world company or person. The statistical method most tools still rest on dates from 1969. For a commercial team it is what keeps an account's history in one place, and what stops two agents treating one buyer as two.

entry.title: Prompt Engineering vs Context Engineering
entry.summary: Prompt engineering is the craft of writing and structuring instructions for a model. Context engineering is the wider job of deciding what the model sees at every step: instructions, retrieved records, tool results and history. Prompting fixes format and tone; context fixes accuracy. For agents and commercial work, context is usually the bigger lever.
